name: Reverse Psychology
description: A persuader deliberately recommends or allows the opposite of the desired outcome in hopes that the target will push back and choose the originally desired behavior instead. It is a tactic, not a basic cognitive mechanism by itself.
design_relevance_note: Occasionally invoked in growth copy, youth-facing warnings, anti-marketing, and community/game messaging, but the evidence base is much thinner and narrower than the popular phrase suggests. In product work it is usually better treated as a possible tactic riding on reactance, not as a standalone law.
myth_risk_note: No peer-reviewed empirical evidence was found for reverse psychology as a general persuasion principle in consumer choice, marketing, or everyday decision-making. The existing corpus backing (Peluso & Freund 2023, paradoxical interventions in psychotherapy) is real but narrow and clinically specialized -- paradoxical directives used to interrupt self-maintaining behavioral cycles in therapy. The term is applied colloquially across design and marketing contexts far beyond what this narrow clinical evidence base actually supports.
prevalence_note: A widely recognized plain-language persuasion trope in marketing, parenting, and behavior-change talk, even though it is much less formalized in mainstream UX methods than foot-in-the-door or reactance.

findings.description: A meta-analysis of paradoxical interventions in individual psychotherapy found a large advantage over controls (d = 1.1, k = 17) and a medium advantage over other therapeutic methods (d = 0.49, k = 17), indicating that deliberately prescribing or inviting the opposite of the desired pattern can work in that narrower clinical setting.
findings.effect_size: d = 1.10 vs controls; d = 0.49 vs other therapies; k = 17 in each comparison

applications.title: Patagonia's "Don't Buy This Jacket" sustainability campaign
applications.description: Patagonia ran an advertising campaign built around the headline "Don't Buy This Jacket," urging consumers to reduce their overall consumption and reconsider whether they needed a new jacket at all -- a brand-image-oriented use of reverse psychology, promoting the company's sustainability image and, per marketing-research analysis, its products, by appearing to argue against a purchase rather than for one.
applications.ethical_note: Genuinely double-edged: the campaign's stated message (buy less, reduce consumption) is user- and environment-beneficial on its face, but its use as reverse psychology means the underlying commercial intent is still to promote the brand and its products -- worth flagging as a case where a persuasion technique and a pro-social message are deliberately combined, not a simple beneficial/manipulative split.

applications.title: Visit Oslo's tourism ad complains about the city to make it more appealing
applications.description: A Visit Oslo tourism campaign, created by Oslo-based agency NewsLab, features a real local resident named Halfdan wryly complaining that Oslo is barely a city, that swimming in the city center is 'disgusting,' and comparing it unfavorably to Paris and New York -- using irony and reverse psychology to make Oslo's small-town qualities (compact size, low crowding, chance encounters with the prime minister) sound appealing precisely by having a local voice deny them.
applications.ethical_note: A transparent, self-aware use of reverse psychology in advertising -- the irony is legible to the viewer (a real local visibly performing mock complaints), not a deceptive claim, distinct from reverse-psychology applications that rely on the target not recognizing the technique being used on them.
